text: summary Engineers learn from other people's crashes — if those crashes have been analyzed. This module takes three public investigations by government boards — the Matternet M2 in Zurich 2019, ArduCopter-based platform, failure due to vibration and EKF , the Alauda Airspeeder Mk II at Goodwood 2019, link loss and a kill switch that didn't work and the Freefly Alta X in Henley 2022, battery depletion — and breaks down each one using the same scheme: symptom → cause → what you see in the log → consequences → what to change in configuration and procedures. Each case ends with a line for your checklist. theory The analysis scheme Board reports AAIB in the UK, STSB/SUST in Switzerland, NTSB in the USA are written with the same logic, and that logic is your tool too: 1. Symptom — what the operator saw. 2. Sequence — events in time order from logs and telemetry. 3. Cause — technical what failed and systemic why it was possible . 4. What you see in the data — specific log messages, parameters, values. 5. Consequences — impact energy, who was nearby, what about the zone. 6. Fix — configuration, design, procedure. Distinguish three types of causes: hardware failure a part broke , configuration error a parameter didn't fit the task , operator error a procedure wasn't followed . In real crashes all three are almost always present. Case 1. Matternet M2, Zurich, May 9, 2019 STSB, final report No. 2390, aircraft SUI-9903 Context. A Swiss Post delivery quadcopter on a modified ArduCopter based on 3.5.0-rc5 , three IMUs, a flight termination system FTS with a parachute. Return flight without payload. Sequence. Takeoff at 10:37:35. After ~50 s, vibration rose on all three IMUs accelerations in places 30 m/s² , and IMU3 produced sharp deviations while IMU1 and IMU2 showed consistent values; the aircraft started oscillating in pitch. At 10:38:46 the log shows EKFCHECK_BAD_VARIANCE ; the error handler activated the FTS at ~185 m above the takeoff point ~100 m above ground : all four motors stopped, the parachute deployed. The parachute line snapped at its attachment on the aircraft; uncontrolled fall, destroyed at 10:38:48. The site: a forest, ~50 m from a group of children with their teachers, who didn't hear the warning signal. Causes. Technical: increasing vibration of undetermined origin probably a resonance from an external factor — prop damage or a bird strike combined with insufficient robustness of the firmware against such an event. Systemic: the modified ArduCopter could run only two EKF lanes, EK2_IMU_MASK = 5 IMU1 and IMU3, without IMU2 — the faulty sensor couldn't be isolated; the FTS triggered an uncontrolled descent right away instead of attempting a controlled flight termination. The parachute line had been damaged by a sharp edge of the aluminum attachment even before deployment and didn't survive the jerk. What you see in the log. VIBE rises on all IMUs, but the data of one IMU diverges sharply from the other two a sign of a local source or sensor, not the frame as a whole ; EKF innovations grow → EKFCHECK_BAD_VARIANCE ; switch to the FTS. Consequences. Impact energy ≈ 118 J without payload above the 80 J accepted as the threshold for serious injury . The delivery program was suspended. Seven safety recommendations. Fixes the real ones . EK2_IMU_MASK = 3 two healthy IMUs + the ability to isolate , checking both EKF lanes at arming, a second safety line and a redesigned attachment, a 100 dB siren, a log analysis tool, parachute compliance with ASTM F3322, maximum speed reduced from 20 to 16 m/s. Board recommendation No. 591: pursue a redundant propulsion concept the analysis noted that layouts with 6 or more motors have a significantly lower probability of failure . Line for your checklist: “Per-IMU vibration in the log checked after every mechanical change; behavior on EKF failsafe known and tested in SITL”. Case 2. Alauda Airspeeder Mk II, Goodwood, July 4, 2019 AAIB, report 03/2021 Context. A 95 kg demonstration multirotor, an in-house flight controller with two IMUs, no GNSS and no RTH, controlled with a FrSky Taranis X9D radio + an R9M module on 915 MHz 10 mW, FCC mode — a band not permitted for airborne use in the UK . A separate kill switch on 433 MHz LoRa with its own battery, cutting the controller's power through a relay. Sequence. ~65 s after takeoff — a sudden uncommanded transition to level attitude, then link loss. On link loss the controller froze the last throttle commands and held level — the aircraft kept climbing at ~2000 ft/min while rotating at ~40°/s for 4 min 12 s up to ~7900 ft, and entered the controlled airspace of a Gatwick holding area. On the “kill” command the observer activated the switch — with no effect. After the battery was depleted, the aircraft flipped over and fell at ~4500 ft/min into a field 40 m from houses, 700 m outside the authorized area. Impact energy ≈ 24,800 J. No injuries. Causes. The exact cause of the link loss was not determined: there was no onboard recording , the boards were destroyed. Systemic causes found by the board: the link-loss failsafe was designed as “hold throttle” rather than “descend/land”; the kill switch had no feedback loss of its channel wasn't detected , with a relay in the normally closed state a switch failure goes unnoticed until the moment you need it , on a breadboard with jumper wires, activated by a voice command instead of automatically; in the wreckage the relay and the power wire were disconnected from the board. The aircraft was not designed or tested to any standard: mounting with Velcro and zip ties, Ethernet cables as ESC signal lines, soldering with jumpers, a 42–58 V battery with no protection at all; no vibration tests, no RF tests. Speed in flight up to 25 m/s against a declared limit of 11 m/s. What you see in the data. Nothing — and that's the main lesson: without a log an investigation ends with the words “not determined”. Fixes. 15 recommendations to the regulator and the operator. For you: failsafe

title: Maintenance and reliability: logs, battery life, maintenance schedule, MTBF
summary: A hobbyist fixes the aircraft after a crash; an operator never lets it get to a crash. The difference is the logbook and the inspection schedule: every flight is recorded, every battery has a history of its cell resistance, props are replaced by a rule rather than “when they crack”, and trends in vi
headings: Logbooks Battery service life Inspection schedule Logs as a maintenance tool Reliability: numbers instead of feelings One-page FMEA Step 1. Logbooks Step 2. Batteries Step 3. Trend from logs Step 4. Schedule and FMEA
text: summary A hobbyist fixes the aircraft after a crash; an operator never lets it get to a crash. The difference is the logbook and the inspection schedule: every flight is recorded, every battery has a history of its cell resistance, props are replaced by a rule rather than “when they crack”, and trends in vibration and motor balance from the logs warn you about wear before it turns into a failure. This module covers aircraft and battery logbooks, battery retirement criteria, an inspection schedule based on flight hours, log analysis as a maintenance tool, and reliability basics — failure rate, MTBF, series and redundant systems — with a calculation that shows why six motors instead of four. theory Logbooks - Aircraft logbook : date, pilot, site, task, flight time min , battery, remarks, link to the log; separately, repairs and replacements what, why, serial numbers . The total flight time of the aircraft and its components motors, ESCs, props is the basis of the inspection schedule. - Battery logbook : battery number sticker , purchase date, cycles, voltage before/after the flight, internal resistance of the cells by date, damage. A number on the battery is mandatory — otherwise the “bad battery” is impossible to pin down. - Format : a spreadsheet or CSV in git next to the aircraft parameters module “Configs in CI” — you get history and search for free. Battery service life - Internal resistance IR of each cell is the main indicator. Measure it with a charger that has an IR function compare using the same device at the same temperature . Rising IR means less output under load and more heating. - Retirement criteria guidelines, check with the manufacturer : cell IR has grown to roughly 1.5–2 times the new value; cell imbalance after charging and resting is more than ~0.03–0.05 V; puffing; capacity below ~80 % of rated; mechanical damage after a crash. A puffed or damaged battery: discharge it and dispose of it properly, do not fly it. - Storage : 3.80–3.85 V per cell storage , cool, in a fireproof bag or box; do not keep them fully charged for more than a few days. - Operating practice : do not discharge below the landing threshold module “Power” , do not charge them hot or cold, use balance charging. Inspection schedule When What Criterion --- --- --- Before every flight props, prop and motor mounting, battery and connector, antennas, straps cracks and chips, play, connector heating After every flight motor and ESC temperature by touch, props, frame, logbook entry one motor noticeably hotter than the others — take it apart After any impact props all of them, not only the broken one , frame, motors for play and binding, check calibrations a prop that touched something — replace it Every ~10–20 h motor bearings spin by hand — grinding, play , frame screws, soldering and connectors, flight controller dampers grinding and play — replace the bearings or the motor Every ~50 h or per season full teardown: wiring, insulation, power connectors, planned firmware update signs of heating, chafing The intervals are starting values; your own come from the logbook: if bearings die within 30 h, the schedule is 20. Logs as a maintenance tool A log is not only “why it crashed” but also “what is wearing out”: - Vibration VIBE in ArduPilot, gyro in Betaflight Blackbox : growth from flight to flight with the same props — bearings, a prop, a loose mount. - Motor balance RCOU / motor n : one motor consistently higher than the others in hover — it is weaker wear, prop or the aircraft is out of balance. - Compass MAG : increased current-induced interference after wiring repairs. - Battery BAT : voltage sag at the same current grows — the battery resistance is growing. A trend matters more than a single value: one point is noise, five points are wear. Reliability: numbers instead of feelings - Failure rate λ — failures per hour roughly constant during normal operation . MTBF = 1/λ — mean time between failures. An MTBF of 1000 h does not mean “1000 h without failures”: the probability of running t hours without a failure is R t = e^ −λt , and for 1000 h that is only 37 %. - Bathtub curve : at the start, early failures defects, cold solder joints → normal operation → wear-out. Hence acceptance testing of new aircraft ground test, first flights low and close and replacement by service life before the wear-out zone. - Series system — failure of any component = failure of the system: R = R₁·R₂·…·Rₙ. For motors, a quadcopter is a series system of four: R = r⁴. - Redundancy — the system works as long as at least one of the duplicates is alive: R = 1 − 1 − r ². A hexacopter that can make it home on five motors is “5 out of 6 needed”: R = r⁶ + 6·r⁵· 1 − r . But the ability to survive a motor failure depends on the frame, thrust-to-weight ratio and firmware — you test it, you don't assume it module “Redundancy” . - Example : motor λ = 1/1000 h illustrative . Over 100 h of flight time without replacement: quad R = e^ −0.4 ≈ 0.67, a hexa that survives one failure ≈ 0.90. The same calculation shows why replacing motors by service life raises reliability more than it seems. {{diagram:chart-reliability Probability of avoiding a loss due to motor failure versus flight time: a quad needs all four versus a hexa that survives one failure.}} One-page FMEA For each component: how it can fail → what the pilot will see → what the aircraft will do → how to detect it in advance → what we do. Five rows for the motor, ESC, battery, receiver and GNSS give you a plan of the inspections and checks that actually matter. practice Step 1. Logbooks Set up an aircraft logbook and a battery logbook CSV or spreadsheet with the fields from the theory. Number the batteries with stickers. Enter the recent flights you can reconstruct from the logs. Step 2. Batteries For each battery: the IR of each cell a charger with an IR function, at room temperature , and the cell voltages after charging and 30 min of rest. Mark the batteries that are close to retire

title: Troubleshooting tree: the drone won't take off
summary: Troubleshooting is not a string of guesses but the elimination of branches of a tree, where every step is confirmed by a fact: a multimeter reading, a firmware message, a log line. This module gives you a tree for five typical situations — “won't arm,” “motors don't spin or spin wrong,” “goes crazy
headings: Troubleshooting rules Tree 1. Won't arm Tree 2. Motors don't spin / spin wrong Tree 3. “Goes crazy” on throttle Tree 4. Something burns/smokes when you plug in the battery Tree 5. Loses link or video How to extend the tree Step 1. Work through three faults Step 2. A fact at every step Step 3. Extend the tree Worked record of one case What to record for the three faults Lab
text: summary Troubleshooting is not a string of guesses but the elimination of branches of a tree, where every step is confirmed by a fact: a multimeter reading, a firmware message, a log line. This module gives you a tree for five typical situations — “won't arm,” “motors don't spin or spin wrong,” “goes crazy on throttle,” “ESC/board burns when you plug in the battery,” “loses link or video” — and a rule for adding your own cases to it. Tools: smoke stopper, multimeter, CLI status /pre-arm messages, Blackbox/DataFlash. theory Troubleshooting rules 1. Fact first, hypothesis second. The firmware almost always tells you what's wrong: Betaflight — status in the CLI the Arming disable flags line , INAV — the Status tab and status in the CLI, ArduPilot — PreArm messages in the GCS. Start there, not with resoldering. 2. One change — one test. If you changed two parameters and it started working, you don't know which one helped, and you don't know what you broke. 3. From cheap to expensive. Visual inspection and the multimeter come before the oscilloscope and replacing the board. 4. Safety at every step. Props off for anything involving the motors. The first power-up after any soldering goes through a smoke stopper. 5. Write down the path. Steps with their results go into a note; the cause you found goes into the tree and into the vehicle's log. Tree 1. Won't arm Read the reason: Betaflight CLI → status → Arming disable flags: ... . The CLI prints short names from runtime_config.c FAILSAFE, CALIB, NO_ACC_CAL, CMS, BOOTGRACE, MOTOR_PROTO, DSHOT_TELEM, ARMSWITCH in 4.5 / ARM_SWITCH in 2025.12+ ; below, some flags are named as in the documentation. The most common ones: - RXLOSS / RX_FAILSAFE — the receiver isn't delivering channels. → Port and protocol UART, CRSF/SBUS, inversion for SBUS on F4 , bind, receiver power 5 V with a multimeter , the Receiver tab — do the channels move? - THROTTLE — throttle is above minimum. → Stick calibration in the radio, min_check , channel reversal. - ANGLE — the vehicle is tilted more than small_angle . → The surface, accelerometer calibration. - CALIBRATING / ACC_CALIBRATION / NOGYRO — the gyro isn't calibrated or isn't detected. → Keep it still at power-up; NOGYRO — a hardware problem or the wrong firmware target. - ARM_SWITCH — the arm switch was on when power was applied. → Switch it off, then on. - MSP / CLI / CMS_MENU — the configurator is connected or the OSD menu is open. → Unplug USB, exit the menu. - NOPREARM — a prearm mode is configured but not activated. - DSHOT_TELEM before 4.5 — RPMFILTER — the RPM filter is enabled but there's no ESC telemetry bidirectional DShot isn't supported by the ESC firmware or isn't enabled . - BOOT_GRACE_TIME — just wait a few seconds after power-up. - MOTOR_PROTOCOL — no motor protocol selected. INAV: the Status tab shows the reasons Navigation is unsafe, Compass not calibrated, Hardware failure... . ArduPilot: PreArm: ... in the GCS — each line names the culprit Compass not calibrated, Gyros inconsistent, RC not calibrated, Throttle below failsafe, GPS: No Fix, Battery failsafe, etc. ; don't disable the checks in ARMING_SKIPCHK before 4.7 — ARMING_CHECK — fix the cause. {{diagram:arming-tree Tree 1 as a diagram: flag → cause → check.}} Tree 2. Motors don't spin / spin wrong Props off. - No motor responds in the Motors tab. → Does the protocol DShot300/600 and motor_pwm_protocol match the ESC? → Are the ESCs getting power voltage at the pads ? → Are the signal wires on the right pads resource MOTOR ? → Do the ESCs beep when power is applied startup tune ? If not, the ESC is dead or has no power. - One motor doesn't spin, the others do. → Swap its signal wire with a working one: if the problem moved with the wire — it's the signal/FC pad; if it stayed — it's the ESC or the motor. → Is the resistance of all three motor phases the same? → Phase solder joints a cold joint is typical . - The motor twitches but won't start. → Lost contact on one phase solder joint, chafed wire or a damaged ESC. → Continuity-test the phases, wiggle them. - Spinning the wrong way / wrong order. → Motors tab: check the number and direction of each one against the frame diagram; change the direction in the ESC firmware BLHeli Suite/Configurator or by swapping two phases. The “props in/out” direction must be consistent across all four. - The drone flips over on takeoff. → This is Tree 2: order/direction or the wrong mixer mixer isn't for your frame . Tree 3. “Goes crazy” on throttle Symptom: it hovers fine, shakes above 60–70% throttle, motors are hot, the drone behaves unpredictably. - Do you have a Blackbox log? If not, record one; otherwise you're guessing. Gyro spectrum: a huge peak at the motor frequency → mechanics imbalance, props, motor bearing play ; wideband noise that grows with throttle → vibration + insufficient filtering; a peak that doesn't move with throttle → frame resonance. - Gyro noise grew after a replacement/repair? → Is there a capacitor on the power bus? Its lead solder joints, its capacitance. → FC mounting dampers, taut wires . - ESC desync a motor suddenly loses RPM, a jerk, then it recovers; in the log — an eRPM dip on one motor : → ESC settings timing, demag , DShot too fast for long wires, a damaged motor; drop the protocol to DShot300, check the phases. - Voltage sag: in the log VBAT drops below the threshold under throttle → the BEC reboots the FC instant loss of control or the ESCs go into protection. → Connector, battery, solder joints. - PID/filters : too much D or P with insufficient filtering → oscillations at high throttle, where there's more noise. → Filters based on the spectrum, then reduce D. - Interference on the receiver from the VTX at full power LQ drops with throttle — rare, but it happens with ripple on the VTX supply : → a VTX power filter, spacing the antennas apart. Tree 4. Something burns/smokes when you plug in the battery Disconnect immediately. From here on — only through a smoke stopper a bulb/lim

title: Onboard power circuit design
summary: An aircraft has several power buses with different requirements: the motor power bus tolerates sags and ripple, but the flight controller, receiver, GPS and camera don't. This module teaches you to compute the currents per branch, pick a BEC by current and voltage, pick wire gauge by current and len
headings: Load map Linear vs switching BEC Sag and internal resistance Ripple and the capacitor Protection Wire gauges Step 1. Power tree Step 2. Choosing BECs and wire gauges Step 3. Capacitor Step 4. Protection Step 5. Measure (link to the measurements module)
text: summary An aircraft has several power buses with different requirements: the motor power bus tolerates sags and ripple, but the flight controller, receiver, GPS and camera don't. This module teaches you to compute the currents per branch, pick a BEC by current and voltage, pick wire gauge by current and length, understand where sags and ripple come from and why a low-ESR capacitor on the bus isn't an option but part of the circuit. Separately — protection: smoke stopper, fuse, reverse polarity. theory Load map Before choosing components, draw the power tree: battery → power bus → ESC ×4…8, 5 V BEC, 9–12 V BEC → loads. Typical currents: {{diagram:power-tree Power tree: from the battery to the power bus and separate BECs; each load with its own current.}} Load Voltage Typical current --- --- --- FC + gyro 5 V 3.3 internal 0.1–0.2 A ELRS receiver 5 V 0.1–0.3 A on-board TX module up to 0.5 GPS with compass 5 V 3.3 0.05–0.1 A Digital video system air unit 9–12 V 0.5–1.2 A, higher peaks Analog VTX 800 mW–1 W 9–12 V / 5 V 0.4–0.7 A Servos wing 5–6 V / 7.4 V 0.5–1 A each while moving Companion Pi 4/5 5 V 1–3 A, peaks up to 5 Lighting/LEDs 5 V 0.06 A per LED Add them up with a 50% margin: a 5 V BEC on an aircraft with GPS, receiver and FC and no companion — 1 A is enough; with a Raspberry you need a separate 3–5 A BEC. Linear vs switching BEC - Linear LDO — dumps the excess voltage as heat: at 6S 25 V → 5 V and 0.5 A it dissipates 10 W. Unsuitable for high voltages and currents, but has no ripple — good for the gyro and RF. - Switching buck — 85–95% efficiency, but produces ripple at the switching frequency hundreds of kHz and its harmonics; a bad buck next to the receiver means lost LQ. Flight controllers have a filtered 5 V / 9 V buck. - A good trick: buck down to 5.5–6 V, then an LDO to 5 V for the sensitive part many FCs are built this way: 3.3 V for the gyro through an LDO . Sag and internal resistance Voltage under load U = E − I·R_int. R_int of a 6S 4P Li-Ion battery ≈ 20–40 mΩ per cell → 30–60 mΩ per pack R × 6 / 4 ; at 60 A the sag is 1.8–3.6 V. Plus the wires: 12 AWG ≈ 5.2 mΩ/m, 14 AWG ≈ 8.3, 16 AWG ≈ 13.2. 20 cm out and back of 14 AWG at 60 A is 0.2 V, which is small; but an XT60 connector with oxidized contacts can add more. The sag isn't dangerous in itself, but because the BEC on the flight controller gets an input voltage below its threshold some bucks shut off below 7–8 V on 2S — an FC reboot in flight. Ripple and the capacitor ESCs switch the windings at tens of kHz, and the current in the battery wires jerks. The inductance of the wires L ≈1 µH per meter turns dI/dt into voltage spikes: U = L·dI/dt. These are ripple and spikes on the power bus that pass into the FC supply, into the gyro noise in the log and into the video lines . The fix is a low-ESR electrolytic or polymer capacitor right on the ESC/PDB power pads: 470–1000 µF at 35 V for 4S, 1000 µF at 50 V for 6S ≥ 30% voltage margin . It acts as a local source: it delivers energy on the edge and absorbs the spike. Short leads — otherwise the lead inductance spoils the effect. Protection - Smoke stopper — a bulb or a resistor/current limiter in series with the positive lead at the first power-up. A short circuit — the bulb lights up, the aircraft doesn't smoke. - Fuse — on large aircraft on the power bus not on the motors — the current is too high and pulsed and on the companion bus. - Reverse polarity — XT60/XT30 protect by their shape, but soldering one backwards kills the board in a second. A Schottky diode in series 0.3–0.5 V drop or a P-MOSFET ideal diode for low-voltage branches. - Connectors : XT30 up to ~15–30 A continuous, XT60 ~30 A continuous briefly up to ~60 A , XT90 ~45 A continuous; AS150/XT150 for high currents. An underloaded connector heats up, a hot one oxidizes, an oxidized one heats up even more. Wire gauges {{widget:wire-drop}} Rule of thumb for short runs on board: 12 AWG up to ~60–80 A, 14 AWG up to ~40–50 A, 16 AWG up to ~25 A, 18 AWG up to ~15 A, 20–22 AWG — signal and 5 V branches up to 2–3 A. The criteria are insulation heating and the acceptable drop; long wires on a wing — one size up. practice Step 1. Power tree Draw the tree for your build with the current on each branch from the table and datasheets . The 5 V total and the 9–12 V total — separately. Step 2. Choosing BECs and wire gauges For each branch: BEC type buck/LDO , rating ≥ 1.5 × the total, input voltage with margin for a fully charged 6S 25.2 V . Wire gauge — from the table. Step 3. Capacitor Choose the capacitance and voltage, solder it to the ESC/PDB pads with leads no longer than 10–15 mm. Record a hover log before/after: gyro noise in the band above 300 Hz spectrum should drop. Step 4. Protection A smoke stopper at every first power-up after soldering. Check with a multimeter that there's no short between + and − before connecting the battery the resistance shouldn't be below hundreds of ohms; with a capacitor it rises at first . Step 5. Measure link to the measurements module Sag under load: battery voltage with no load and in hover from the log . 5 V ripple — with an oscilloscope with AC coupling: typically < 50–100 mV p-p. diagnostics - Symptom: the FC reboots on a sharp throttle punch - Possible cause: a sag below the BEC threshold or a bad connector contact. - What to do: VBAT log, check the XT connector, the capacitor, a higher-capacity/fresher battery. - Symptom: lines in the analog video on throttle - Possible cause: power bus ripple gets into the VTX. - What to do: a capacitor on the power bus, power the VTX from a filtered BEC, an LC filter. - Symptom: gyro noise went up after replacing the ESC - Possible cause: a different switching frequency, no capacitor. - What to do: a capacitor on the pads, check the FC grounding. - Symptom: the BEC is hot - Possible cause: a linear BEC with a high input voltage, or current above the rating. - What to do: recompute the dissipated power, a buck instead of an LDO, offload the branch.

title: Measurements: multimeter, oscilloscope, logic analyzer
summary: What separates an engineer from an assembler is that the engineer measures instead of assuming. This module is about three instruments: the multimeter (voltage, current, continuity, resistance), the oscilloscope (sags, ripple, PWM/DShot waveforms, noise) and the logic analyzer (decoding UART, I2C, S
headings: Multimeter Oscilloscope DShot on the oscilloscope Logic analyzer Measurement safety Step 1. Map of measurement points Step 2. Sag under load Step 3. BEC ripple Step 4. DShot and UART with the analyzer Step 5. Report A decoded DShot frame What you should get and what to record
text: summary What separates an engineer from an assembler is that the engineer measures instead of assuming. This module is about three instruments: the multimeter voltage, current, continuity, resistance , the oscilloscope sags, ripple, PWM/DShot waveforms, noise and the logic analyzer decoding UART, I2C, SPI, DShot . What to measure, how to connect, how not to fry the instrument or the aircraft, and how to read the result. theory Multimeter - Voltage — in parallel with the load. Useful: the voltage of each battery cell balance , 5 V and 9 V on the BEC under load. - Continuity — before applying power: + to − on the power bus, 5 V to GND. A beep = a short. With a capacitor the resistance rises as it charges — that's normal. - Current — in series, through the 10 A jack; anything more — only with a clamp meter or through the FC current sensor. Never measure voltage in current mode: that's a short circuit through the meter. - Resistance — checking motor windings three identical values of a few tenths of an ohm , a broken wire. - Limitation: a multimeter shows the average/RMS; it doesn't see brief sags and ripple. Oscilloscope Shows voltage over time. For on-board work 2 channels and 50–100 MHz are enough; a USB oscilloscope will do too. - Sag : a channel on the power bus, timebase 100 ms/div, trigger on the falling edge; punch the throttle — you see the depth and duration of the dip. - Ripple : AC coupling removes the DC component , 20–50 mV/div, timebase 10–50 µs/div — you see the ESC/BEC switching frequency and the p-p amplitude. Measure with a short ground spring instead of the long alligator clip — otherwise you pick up noise from the probe itself. - Signals : PWM servos — a 1–2 ms pulse every 20 ms 50 Hz ; UART — bursts of bits with idle at the high level; DShot — bursts of 16 pulses of different widths. - A ×10 probe reduces the load on the circuit and extends the bandwidth; for 3.3 V logic it's mandatory. DShot on the oscilloscope A DShot frame is 16 bits: 11 throttle bits, 1 telemetry bit, 4 CRC bits. Each bit is a pulse: “1” is long ~75% of the bit period , “0” is short ~37% . DShot600 is 600 kbit/s, a bit ≈ 1.67 µs, a frame ≈ 27 µs. On screen — a burst of 16 pulses repeating at the PID loop rate for example, every 125 µs at 8 kHz . Problems you can see: ringing on the edges long wire, no termination , a level that doesn't reach 3.3 V weak driver , dropped frames. Logic analyzer Records digital levels on many channels and decodes protocols. A cheap 8-channel 24 MHz one with software like PulseView/sigrok is enough for UART up to 1 Mbaud, I2C at 400 kHz, SPI up to a few MHz and DShot600 you need ≥ 4–5 samples per bit — 12–24 MHz is better . - UART : connect to the TX line and GND, set the baud rate 115200 for MSP/CRSF — 420000 for CRSF! , the decoder shows the bytes. You can see: the wrong baud rate garbage , inversion SBUS is an inverted UART at 100000 8E2 . - I2C : SDA and SCL, the decoder shows addresses and ACK/NACK. A NACK on an address — the sensor isn't there or the address is different; no pull-up — the lines don't go high. - SPI : CLK, MOSI, MISO, CS — reading the gyro registers. - A common ground with the aircraft — always. Levels are 3.3 V; most analyzers tolerate 5 V lines, 12 V — no. Measurement safety - Props off for any measurement on ESCs/motors. - The oscilloscope ground is tied to protective earth: on a circuit that isn't referenced to earth battery powered that's fine; on a mains-powered supply you must not clip the probe ground to a point that carries a potential. - The probe never touches two pins at once: tiny FC pads are the number one way to cause a short with the instrument. {{diagram:measure-tools Which instrument for which question: values — multimeter, waveform — oscilloscope, protocol — logic analyzer.}} practice Step 1. Map of measurement points On the aircraft's schematic mark: the power bus, the 5 V output, the 9 V output, the receiver UART, DShot on one motor, the compass I2C. Find convenient pads. Step 2. Sag under load Without props the measurement is meaningless — use the log VBAT in hover or an oscilloscope on a test stand with a real load aircraft tied down, props on, short throttle pulses, extremely carefully and with an observer . Record: U with no load, U at maximum, duration of the dip. Step 3. BEC ripple AC coupling, 5 V under receiver/GPS load. Record p-p and frequency. Compare with/without a capacitor on the power bus. Step 4. DShot and UART with the analyzer Capture a DShot frame at low throttle without props: decode the 16 bits by hand, compute the throttle value DShot 48–2047 and check the CRC. Capture CRSF between the receiver and the FC at 420000 baud: find the channels frame type 0x16 . Step 5. Report A table: point, instrument, value, normal range, conclusion. A decoded DShot frame Throttle value 1046, telemetry bit 0. Twelve bits: 10000010110 0 . CRC = v ⊕ v 4 ⊕ v 8 & 0xF = 6 0110 , where v is those 12 bits. The frame is 16 bits 1000001011000110 0x82C6 . On the oscilloscope each DShot600 bit lasts ≈ 1.67 µs: “1” is a long high pulse, “0” a short one. From your captured frame compute the value and the CRC and compare them with the throttle you set. What you should get and what to record - Sag under load: VBAT in the log in hover and at a short burst of full throttle — the difference and how it relates to the internal resistance from the “Electricity” module. - BEC ripple: the swing p-p on 5 V under load — tens of millivolts for a good BEC. Hundreds of millivolts mean interference in the video and sensor glitches. Record p-p and frequency with and without the capacitor on the power bus. - CRSF: the channels frame starts with the address byte 0xC8 , then the length 0x18 24 and the type 0x16 RC channels packed : 16 channels of 11 bits each. - Table: point, instrument, value, normal range, conclusion — one row per measurement. Without the “normal range” column a measurement tells you nothing. The lab is passed when the sag under load is mea

title: Li-Ion and LiFePO4 packs: cells, welding, BMS
summary: LiPo is the norm for 5" and anything that needs 20C+, but long-range wings, 7–10" long range and heavy-lift X8s fly on Li-Ion 18650/21700, while ground stations and heavy platforms run on LiFePO4. This module compares the three chemistries in numbers, teaches you to work out the S/P configuration fo
headings: Three chemistries in numbers S/P configuration Spot welding BMS, balancer and the drone Internal resistance and health Step 1. Pick the chemistry for the job Step 2. S/P calculation Step 3. Welding design Step 4. Pack test
text: summary LiPo is the norm for 5" and anything that needs 20C+, but long-range wings, 7–10" long range and heavy-lift X8s fly on Li-Ion 18650/21700, while ground stations and heavy platforms run on LiFePO4. This module compares the three chemistries in numbers, teaches you to work out the S/P configuration for current and capacity with internal resistance in mind, build a pack by spot welding nickel strip without overheating the cell, pick a BMS and balancer so they don't cut power to the aircraft in flight, and measure the real capacity and sag with a cycle under load. theory Three chemistries in numbers Parameter LiPo graphite/LCO-NMC Li-Ion 18650/21700 NMC/NCA LiFePO4 --- --- --- --- Cell nominal 3.7 V 4.2 full, 3.3–3.5 land 3.6 V 4.2 full, 2.5–3.0 land 3.2 V 3.65 full, 2.5 land Specific energy 150–200 Wh/kg 220–270 Wh/kg high-capacity 21700 90–140 Wh/kg Continuous current 20–100C a 1300 mAh 75C pack ≈ 100 A 3–10C per cell P42A: 45 A at 4.2 Ah; 40T: 35 A at 4 Ah; VTC6: 15 A per datasheet, 30 A with an 80 °C cutoff, at 3 Ah 1–3C, high-current ones up to 10C Cycle life 150–300 cycles to 80% 300–500 2000–4000 Internal resistance 1–5 mΩ/cell 15–40 mΩ/cell 5–20 mΩ 26650 Safety catches fire easily, puffs burns, but protected by the can; CID/PTC in “protected” versions very tolerant of overcharge and temperature Where it fits racing, freestyle, anything with T/W 3 long range, wings, heavy-lift, companion power ground equipment, heavy slow platforms, stationary Rule: Li-Ion wins when the average pack current is ≤ 1–2C and the flight is longer than 15 minutes. If hover needs 3C, go LiPo. S/P configuration - S sets the voltage: 6S Li-Ion = 21.6 V nominal, 25.2 full, 18 V to land 3.0 V/cell , 15 V is the absolute limit. - P sets the current and capacity: 4P of P42A = 16.8 Ah, 4 × 45 = 180 A continuous per datasheet, but in practice limited by heating and sag. - Sag : R of the pack = R of the cell × S / P. 6S4P P42A ≈ 25 mΩ × 6 / 4 ≈ 38 mΩ plus strip and connections — +10–20 mΩ . At 60 A the sag is ≈ 2.3–3.5 V — almost 1 cell “lost” under load. That's why for the same job you size Li-Ion with margin on P, not “right at the datasheet current”. - Heat : P = I²·R on the pack: 60 A × 60 A × 0.05 Ω = 180 W over the whole pack — noticeable heating in 10 minutes. Rule of thumb: average current ≤ 1.5C for 21700 without forced cooling. - Mass budget : 6S4P 21700 ≈ 24 × 70 g = 1.7 kg + strip/case ≈ 1.85 kg for 363 Wh ≈ 195 Wh/kg including hardware . Spot welding You must not solder to cells: overheating the terminal damages the separator and the protection. Weld with nickel strip: - Strip : pure nickel not nickel-plated steel — its resistance is several times higher and it rusts . A 0.15 × 8 mm cross-section carries roughly 7–10 A per path continuously; for high-current packs use 0.2 × 10 mm, “doubled” strip or a copper bus bar with a nickel layer, or parallel paths. - Welder : a capacitor/supercapacitor or transformer welder; tune it on scraps: a weld should tear the strip leaving a crater, not peel off. Two electrodes on the same side, 2–4 welds per cell. - Order : welding layout on paper → cells of equal capacity and voltage spread ≤ 0.02 V → insulator rings on the positive terminals → parallel groups → series links → balance wires from each group → heat shrink/case with air for cooling. - Safety : shorting a 21700 through nickel strip means hundreds of amps and a burn; work one connection at a time, no metal tools over the assembled part, safety glasses, sand nearby, a non-combustible box and a bucket of water for cooling class D is for metallic lithium, and Li-Ion has none . BMS, balancer and the drone A BMS protects against overcharge, overdischarge, overcurrent and temperature. For flight a classic BMS is dangerous: a discharge cutoff on current/temperature in the air = a crash. Options: 1. No BMS on board — balancing through the balance connector at charging like LiPo , voltage monitoring by the flight controller voltage failsafe . The standard for flying packs. 2. Charge-only BMS : balancer and protection while charging, discharge goes direct. Good for stationary and ground use. 3. Smart BMS with configurable thresholds JK/Jikong and similar, with a 1–2 A active balancer and Bluetooth : for ground stations and heavy slow platforms; for flight — only with discharge protection disabled and with an understanding of the consequences. An active balancer moves energy between groups is needed for large capacity and infrequent full charges; a passive one burns the excess on resistors is enough for 4–6S flying packs balanced regularly. Internal resistance and health The charger shows IR per cell: a new 21700 ≈ 15–25 mΩ; a rise to 50+ is end of life for high-current work. A difference between groups 30% means a weak group — check the welds/cells. LiPo: 1–3 mΩ new, 10+ — time to move it to ground duty. {{diagram:chemistry-choice Choosing a chemistry: LiPo when you need current, Li-Ion when you need energy, LiFePO4 when you need cycle life and safety.}} practice Step 1. Pick the chemistry for the job For your aircraft: average hover/cruise current from the log, the desired flight time, the mass. Work out the C-rate for the LiPo and Li-Ion candidates. If the average current is ≤ 1.5C on Li-Ion, go on with Li-Ion. Step 2. S/P calculation Pick a cell datasheet: capacity, continuous current, IR . P ≥ maximum current / 0.6 × cell current — a 40% margin for heating and sag. Work out the pack R, the sag at maximum and in hover, the heat, the mass and Wh/kg. Compare with LiPo. Step 3. Welding design Layout: cell arrangement, strip direction, path cross-section for the group current, balance wire points, connector XT60/XT90 depending on current , an output fuse. text: summary The aircraft is a tightly packed box of interference sources ESCs, power wires, buck converters, VTX, companion and victims compass, GPS, receiver, gyro . This module explains the mechanisms: the magnetic field of a current, radiation from switching edges, and conducted noise on the power and ground lines; it teaches three techniques twist, shield, separate and, most importantly, how to measure the effect from logs: the compass via MAG / compassmot , GPS via satellite count and HDOP, the receiver via LQ/RSSI. theory Three interference paths 1. The magnetic field of a current — around a wire carrying current I, at distance r, the field is B = μ₀·I/ 2π·r . At 60 A and 5 cm that's 240 µT, 5 times the Earth's magnetic field ~50 µT . A compass 5 cm from a power wire is useless on throttle. The field falls off as 1/r: twice as far means half as strong; a twisted pair with opposing currents cancels the field almost completely. 2. Radiation from switching edges — ESCs and bucks switch current in tens of nanoseconds; sharp edges contain harmonics up to hundreds of MHz. The wires act as antennas. Victims: GPS 1.5 GHz, signal at −130 dBm — the weakest on board , the 900 MHz/2.4 GHz receiver, analog video. 3. Conducted interference — through shared power and ground wires. Buck ripple gets into the receiver's supply; ESC current through a shared ground creates a potential difference between the FC ground and the camera ground — lines in the video. Worked example: the compass and a power wire Current 60 A, Earth's field ~50 µT. Single wire, B = 2·10⁻⁷·I/r: Distance to the compass Single wire Twisted pair 3 mm spacing --- --- --- 5 cm 240 µT ×5 the Earth's field 14 µT 10 cm 120 µT 3.6 µT 20 cm 60 µT 0.9 µT The field of a pair with opposing currents is the difference between the fields of the two wires: B ≈ 2·10⁻⁷·I·d/r², falling off as 1/r², not 1/r. Hence two rules that do more than any shielding: power + and − always run together twisted or tightly bundled , and the compass sits at least 10 cm from the power bus, preferably on a mast. The magnetic field of a DC current is not shielded by foil — only by distance, geometry or mu-metal. Current-based compass compensation If you can't separate them, ArduPilot can subtract the interference: compassmot with props on, the vehicle rigidly secured measures the field on board as a function of current and writes coefficients to COMPASS_MOT_X/Y/Z ; the mode is COMPASS_MOTCT 1 — by throttle, 2 — by current, needs a current sensor . This compensates the linear part of the interference; the nonlinear part saturation, eddy currents it does not. If the interference is above ~30 % of the Earth's field after compensation, the compass still has to be moved. GPS: look at C/N0, not just the satellites Satellite count and HDOP drop late. The first thing to react to interference is the signal-to-noise ratio of each satellite C/N0, dB·Hz : under open sky, 35–45 dB·Hz for visible satellites. If turning on the VTX or companion lowers the C/N0 of all satellites by 5–10 dB at once, that's interference on board, not the sky. To look: u-center through the flight controller passthrough SERIAL_PASS1 / SERIAL_PASS2 and SERIAL_PASSTIMO in ArduPilot, the serialpassthrough command in Betaflight/INAV , the Satellite Level view. Victims and their symptoms - Compass : heading changes with throttle; in ArduPilot compassmot shows the % of interference; in the log MAG.MagX/Y/Z correlate with CTUN.ThO . Above 30% is bad, you need to separate. - GPS : satellite count drops when the VTX/companion is turned on, HDOP rises, GPS.NSats , GPS.HDop . Typical culprits: USB 3.0 harmonics at 1.5 GHz , cameras, HDMI, a buck next to the GPS antenna. - Receiver : LQ drops while RSSI is normal — a wideband noise source near the antenna VTX, companion . Sometimes RSSI “rises” from interference: the receiver sees the noise as signal. - Gyro : noise in the log at the buck switching frequency — rare, but it happens with poor layout. - Video : lines on throttle — conducted ripple; “snow” — radiation. Techniques - Twist the power + and −: opposing currents cancel the magnetic field; twisting signal wires with ground reduces pickup. - Separate : compass and GPS on a mast pointing up 10–15 cm of distance gives ×3–5 on the field , receiver antennas away from the VTX and companion, preferably at the other end of the frame. - Shield : copper foil/shielding fabric on the companion and camera, grounded at a single point; ferrite rings on USB/HDMI cables turns through the ring — more turns, stronger suppression . - Filter : an LC filter on the VTX/camera supply, a capacitor on the power bus see power circuit design , an LDO for the receiver. - Single ground : a star from the PDB, not a daisy chain; a cable shield grounded at one end otherwise — a ground loop . Measure, don't guess One change at a time, with a before/after measurement: - compass: compassmot or the correlation of MAG with throttle in the log; - GPS: NSats/HDOP at rest for 5 minutes with the loads turned on and off one by one; - receiver: LQ at 50–100 m with the VTX off/on, companion off/on; - video: an oscilloscope in AC mode on the camera supply. {{diagram:emi-paths Three interference paths and their typical victims: the magnetic field of a current — compass, radiation from switching edges — GPS and receiver, conducted — video and RX power.}} practice Step 1. A map of sources and victims On the aircraft wiring diagram, mark the sources ESCs, power wires, buck, VTX, companion, USB and the victims compass, GPS, RX antennas, camera with distances. Step 2. Compass The safe way is from the log: a 30 s hover with smooth throttle changes, a plot of MAG.MagX/Y/Z and the vector magnitude B against BAT.Curr or CTUN.ThO . Correlation = interference; estimate its size as a percentage of B on the ground. compassmot only with the vehicle rigidly secured, following the ArduPilot instructions, with props on and nobody in the plane of rotation. text: summary The antenna is half of the radio link, and the most underrated half. This module explains dipole, patch, cloverleaf and “T” antennas, the difference between linear and circular polarization, what gain in dBi is and why it always comes at the cost of beamwidth, how to read a radiation pattern and orient antennas on the aircraft and on the ground, what SWR measures and when an antenna is “the wrong one.” It ends with a ground range test. theory How an antenna radiates A half-wave dipole is two conductors, each a quarter wave long. λ = c/f: 2.4 GHz → 12.5 cm quarter 3.1 cm , 915 MHz → 32.8 cm quarter 8.2 cm , 5.8 GHz → 5.2 cm quarter 1.3 cm . An antenna is “tuned” when its size matches the frequency — then the energy goes out into the air instead of reflecting back. Radiation pattern and gain An isotropic radiator an imaginary one radiates equally in all directions — 0 dBi. A real antenna redistributes energy: a dipole gives 2.15 dBi in the plane perpendicular to its axis and nothing along the axis the “donut” . Gain always comes from narrowing the beam. An 8–9 dBi patch covers a sector of ~60–70°, a 12–14 dBi directional Yagi about ~30°. On the aircraft you need an omnidirectional antenna its attitude keeps changing ; on the ground, a directional one, if there's someone to aim it. The main consequence for the aircraft: a dipole/“T” antenna mounted vertically does not radiate up or down. If the aircraft is directly overhead, you get a null. That's why the two receiver antennas diversity are mounted at 90° to each other. Worked example: where the dipole's null is A vertical dipole on the radio, the aircraft at 100 m altitude. Elevation angle θ = atan h/d , angle from the dipole axis is 90° − θ, relative gain ≈ sin² angle from the axis : Aircraft distance Elevation angle Pattern loss --- --- --- 1 km 5.7° 0 dB 300 m 18° −0.5 dB 100 m 45° −3 dB 30 m almost overhead 73° −10.8 dB Takeaway: at long range the dipole works perfectly, and the null happens close in and overhead — where you have plenty of power margin. That's why you hold the radio's antenna side-on to the aircraft don't point its tip at it , and on the aircraft a second antenna at 90° covers the first one's null. What dBi buys you in range +6 dB of gain = ×2 range in free space. An 8 dBi patch on the ground instead of a 2 dBi dipole gives +6 dB — double the range, but only inside the beam sector : once the aircraft leaves the sector, you lose more than you gained. A directional antenna without aiming a tracker or a pilot turning the radio is a trap for flights that go “around in a circle.” Polarization - Linear dipole, “T”, monopole : the field oscillates in one plane. The receiving antenna must be in the same plane: a 90° rotation gives up to 20–30 dB of loss in theory, 10–20 in practice because of reflections. When the aircraft banks, the polarization gets misaligned. - Circular cloverleaf, helical, circularly polarized patch : the field rotates — right-hand RHCP or left-hand LHCP . Antenna orientation barely matters; reflections reverse the direction of rotation and get attenuated less multipath — cleaner video . You pay ~3 dB when receiving circular with a linear antenna and vice versa. RHCP↔LHCP costs 15–20 dB: don't mix them. - For 5.8 GHz video — circular on both ends; for 900 MHz/2.4 GHz RC — linear dipoles mounted orthogonally. SWR and matching SWR shows how much of the power is reflected from the antenna back into the transmitter. 1.0 is ideal; 1.5 — 4% reflected −0.18 dB , 2.0 — 11% −0.5 dB , 3.0 — 25% −1.25 dB . High SWR heats the VTX and can kill it; it affects range less than you'd think as long as it's ≤ 2. It's measured with an antenna analyzer NanoVNA — affordable . An antenna is “the wrong one” when the SWR minimum is not at your frequency trimmed for / designed for another band , the connector is damaged, or the coax ground is torn off. Placement on the aircraft - Antennas go outside the carbon: carbon is a conductor, it shields and detunes the antenna. - Receiver: two antennas at 90°, away from the VTX and power wiring; tail “whiskers” pointing down and back at 45°. - Video: antenna on top or on the bottom so that there is no frame or battery between it and the ground/pilot; for flying far and low — on the bottom. - GPS: on top, ceramic patch horizontal, with a ground plane under it. - Keep the pigtail cable as short as possible: thin RG178 coax loses ~1 dB per 30 cm at 5.8 GHz. Connectors: the quiet cause of a “bad antenna” SMA and RP-SMA look the same, but one has the pin in the plug and the other in the jack: “it screwed on” doesn't mean “it connected” — the center contact may not touch. U.FL/IPEX is rated for a few dozen mating cycles and pops off from vibration if not secured — a drop of glue or heat shrink on the cable. MMCX holds better but also needs cable strain relief. {{diagram:polarization-loss Polarization mismatch loss: matched — 0 dB, linear to circular — 3 dB, crossed or opposite hand — 20 dB and more.}} {{diagram:chart-antenna-patterns Radiation patterns: a vertical dipole has a null along its axis above and below the aircraft , a patch radiates forward in a sector and barely sees backward. Models: dipole sin²θ, patch cos⁴θ with a −20 dB back lobe.}} {{widget:antenna-pol}} practice Step 1. Inventory For every antenna on the aircraft and on the ground: band, type, polarization and the hand of circular , gain, connector SMA/RP-SMA, U.FL/MMCX . Check that polarizations match in every link. Step 2. Orientation Sketch the patterns the dipole donut, the patch sector projected onto the aircraft in typical attitudes: hover, 45° bank, flying out to 1 km at 100 m altitude elevation ~6° . Make sure that in every attitude both ends “see” each other outside a null. Step 3. SWR NanoVNA if you have one : 1. Sweep range: 5.6–6.0 GHz for video or 2.3–2.6 GHz, 850–950 MHz for RC . 2. text: summary “Will it make 10 km?” is a question of arithmetic, not faith. A link budget is a sum in decibels: transmitter power + antenna gains − cable losses − free-space attenuation must be above the receiver sensitivity, with a margin for fading. This module teaches you to calculate it for RC and video, turn the margin into an expected range, set the RSSI warning threshold and compare the calculation with a field test — and shows why 900 MHz goes farther than 2.4 GHz at the same power, and why 5.8 GHz video is the weak link. theory Decibels in five minutes dB is a logarithmic measure of a ratio: 3 dB ≈ ×2 in power, 10 dB = ×10, 20 dB = ×100. dBm is power relative to 1 mW: 0 dBm = 1 mW, 20 dBm = 100 mW, 27 dBm = 500 mW, 30 dBm = 1 W. Doubling the transmitter power gives +3 dB — the same as a slightly better antenna. Doubling the range costs 6 dB see below . Free-space path loss FSPL FSPL dB = 20·log₁₀ d, km + 20·log₁₀ f, MHz + 32.44. Range 915 MHz 2.4 GHz 5.8 GHz --- --- --- --- 1 km 91.7 100.0 107.7 5 km 105.7 114.0 121.7 10 km 111.7 120.0 127.7 30 km 121.2 129.6 137.2 Every doubling of range is +6 dB; going from 915 MHz → 2.4 GHz costs 8.4 dB at the same range, → 5.8 GHz another 7.7 dB. This is the physics of the receiving antenna's aperture, not “penetrating power.” The budget equation Prx = Ptx + Gtx + Grx − Lcable − FSPL − Lextra , margin M = Prx − Ssens. - Ptx — transmitter power in dBm. - G — antenna gain in dBi dipole 2, patch 8, Yagi 12 . - Lcable — pigtails/cables 0.5–2 dB . - Lextra — polarization 3 dB linear↔circular , mismatch, obstacles, the Fresnel zone near the ground flying low over the surface costs another 6–20 dB . - S — receiver sensitivity in dBm for the given mode for ELRS, from the mode table: 2.4 GHz 50 Hz −115, 150 Hz −112, 250 Hz −108, 500 Hz −105; 900 MHz 25 Hz −123, 50 Hz −120, 100 Hz −117, 200 Hz −112 . Margin M: 10–15 dB is the minimum for a reliable link with fading multipath, aircraft maneuvering ; 20 dB is comfortable; 0 is the edge, the link will keep dropping. RC example: ELRS 2.4 GHz, 250 Hz, 250 mW Ptx = 24 dBm, Gtx = 2 radio dipole , Grx = 2 onboard dipole, but we count 0 because of orientation , Lcable = 1, polarization another −3 in banks. Prx at 10 km = 24 + 2 + 0 − 1 − 120 − 3 = −98 dBm. S 250 Hz = −108 → 10 dB margin. Switching to 50 Hz −115 gives 17 dB — or the same reliability at ~22 km. Raising power to 1 W +6 dB is the same as doubling the range. Video example: analog 5.8 GHz 800 mW Ptx = 29 dBm, onboard cloverleaf 2, ground patch 8, cables −1.5, S of a typical analog receiver ≈ −90 dBm video starts getting noisy long before it's lost . At 5 km: 29 + 2 + 8 − 1.5 − 121.7 = −84 dBm → 6 dB margin, the picture will have interference. Digital systems work down to −100…−105 dBm, but cut out abruptly at the threshold. Video almost always limits range before RC does — hence 900 MHz/1.2–1.3 GHz video for long-range flights and directional antennas on the ground. How to turn the budget into an RSSI threshold The ELRS rule: warning when RSSI is ~8–10 dB above the mode's sensitivity; the critical failsafe threshold is at the sensitivity. For 2.4 GHz 250 Hz: warning at −98…−100 dBm, at −105 — turn back. In EdgeTX — a voice warning on RSSI dBm and on LQ <70% at 250 Hz is a reason to worry . Why the calculation doesn't match the field Multipath ground reflections add up out of phase , obstacles in the Fresnel zone the first-zone radius at 2.4 GHz over 5 km is ~12 m: flying low over the ground costs 6–20 dB , onboard interference it reduces effective sensitivity , the real antenna orientation. That's why a range test is mandatory and a 10–15 dB margin is the minimum. {{diagram:link-budget-chain Worked budget example: ELRS 2.4 GHz, 250 mW, 10 km — received power of −98 dBm against a sensitivity of −108 dBm gives a 10 dB margin.}} {{diagram:chart-link-margin Received power from the free-space formula against ELRS sensitivity thresholds the table from the link-elrs module . The margin is the distance from the curve to the threshold; a real flight needs 10–15 dB for fading, antenna rotation and the aircraft body.}} {{widget:link-margin}} practice Step 1. RC budget table For your link: power, mode and its sensitivity, antennas, cables. Calculate the margin at 1, 3, 5, 10 km. Find the range where the margin = 12 dB — that's your working limit. Step 2. Video budget table The same for the video system, with the real sensitivity of the receiver/goggles. Compare the limits: what fails first. Step 3. Thresholds Set an RSSI dBm warning = S + 10 and an LQ warning on the radio; record them in the aircraft's logbook. Failsafe in the firmware is tested. Step 4. Field test A straight-line flight logging RSSI/LQ in the radio or FC log at 500 m, 1, 2 km within permitted limits and area . Compare the measured RSSI with the calculated Prx for the same distances: the difference is your “reality correction,” usually 5–10 dB. Worked example and what to record The module's example: ELRS 2.4 GHz, 250 mW 24 dBm , antennas 2 and 0 dBi, 4 dB of losses cables and polarization , 150 Hz mode sensitivity −112 dBm. Free-space loss at 1 km at 2440 MHz: 20·log10 1 + 20·log10 2440 + 32.44 ≈ 100.2 dB. Received power 24 + 2 + 0 − 4 − 100.2 ≈ −78 dBm, margin ≈ 34 dB. Every doubling of distance takes away 6 dB: a 12 dB margin remains out to ≈ 12–13 km — that's the theoretical limit in free space. The same calculation is in the link budget widget above. - RC and video table: distance, FSPL, received power, margin. Mark the distance where the margin drops to 12 dB. Usually video gives out first, not RC — check whether that's true for you. - Thresholds on the radio. Warning on RSSI = sensitivity + 10 dB here −102 dBm and on LQ. Record the values in the aircraft's logbook. - Field test. The measured RSSI at 500 m, 1 and 2 km is usually 5–10 dB worse than calculated: ground, the Fresnel zone, the airframe, antenna orientation. That difference is your correction — subtract it from the calculated range fo

text: summary Frying a flight controller port is easier than it seems: 5 V on a 3.3 V pin, swapped TX/RX with power coming from two sources, I2C without pull-ups, CAN without a terminator. This module is a practical procedure for connecting any device: identify the interface and levels → find a port and its power → check with a multimeter before power-up → configure the protocol in the firmware → confirm the data with an analyzer. With examples: GPS+compass, rangefinder, ESC telemetry, digital video system, DroneCAN node. theory Three buses and their character Bus Wires Speed Addressing Typical devices Main pitfalls --- --- --- --- --- --- UART TX, RX, GND +power 9600 – 2 Mbaud; GPS 38400–115200, CRSF 420000, MSP 115200 point-to-point GPS, receiver, telemetry, VTX, rangefinder, companion TX↔RX crossed; inversion SBUS ; one port — one device I2C SDA, SCL, GND 100/400 kHz 7-bit address, many devices on the bus compass, barometer, OLED, some rangefinders no pull-ups; identical addresses; long wires 30 cm — trouble SPI CLK, MOSI, MISO, CS up to tens of MHz by CS gyro, OSD, flash, sometimes baro on-board only; almost never brought out CAN DroneCAN CAN_H, CAN_L, GND +power 1 Mbit/s node ID 1–125 GPS/compass, ESC, current sensors, servos, rangefinders no 120 Ω terminators at the ends; twisted pair; identical node IDs Levels and power - FC logic is 3.3 V . Most inputs tolerate 5 V “5V tolerant” , but not all: read the MCU datasheet STM32F4/F7/H7 — most GPIOs are 5V-tolerant, except pins with analog functions . Rule: if in doubt — a 1k/2k divider at the FC input or a level shifter. - Port power : the 5 V and 9 V pads on the FC come from on-board BECs with a limit typically 5 V/2–3 A, 9 V/2–3 A total for all loads . Powering a Raspberry Pi or a digital air unit “from the pad” overloads the BEC; power it from a separate BEC. - Common ground — always. A device with its own power and no common ground with the FC means garbage on the UART or a fried port. - Two power points a device powered from the FC and from the companion's USB at the same time — reverse current through the BEC. A diode or a single power source. UART: details - FC TX → device RX, FC RX ← device TX. - Inversion : SBUS and some protocols are inverted; on an F4 without a hardware inverter you need an external one or a port with an inverter; F7/H7 — software inversion Betaflight serialrx_inverted . CRSF is not inverted, one line in each direction. - Half-duplex : ESC telemetry KISS/BLHeli_32 protocol arrives on one RX pin from all ESCs over a common wire; VTX SmartAudio/Tramp — one wire to the TX pin. - One device per UART except half-duplex protocols designed specifically for that . I2C: details - Pull-ups of 2.2–4.7 kΩ on SDA and SCL to 3.3 V — usually already on the FC; a second device with its own pull-ups lowers the combined resistance — fine down to ~1 kΩ equivalent. - Addresses: compass HMC5883 0x1E, QMC5883 0x0D, IST8310 0x0C/0x0E, baro BMP280 0x76/0x77, MS5611 0x76/0x77. Two devices with the same address — a conflict. - Length: short wires, twisted with ground; on a GPS mast 15–20 cm is fine, 50 cm is already risky drop to 100 kHz . {{diagram:i2c-transaction An I2C transaction bit by bit — exactly what the logic analyzer sees when “the sensor can't be found.”}} DroneCAN: when and how When: the aircraft is large long wires → UART/I2C pick up noise , there are many devices, you need ESC and sensor telemetry on one bus, redundancy. In ArduPilot: CAN_P1_DRIVER = 1 enable port 1 , CAN_D1_PROTOCOL = 1 DroneCAN , reboot; GPS GPS_TYPE = 9 GPS1_TYPE in 4.6+ — DroneCAN, the compass is detected automatically. The bus: twisted pair, 120 Ω terminators at both ends many devices have a terminator jumper , node power per the spec usually 5 V , unique node IDs the autopilot hands them out as a DNA server with dynamic allocation; CAN_D1_UC_NODE is the autopilot's own node ID . Connection procedure always the same 1. Device datasheet: interface, levels, power V, mA , protocol and speed. 2. FC map: a free port, its inverter/power, the BEC limit. 3. Wires labeled; TX/RX crossed; common ground. 4. Before power-up : multimeter — no short from 5 V/3.3 V to GND, the device's power will come from the right pad. 5. Power up through a smoke stopper. The voltage at the device is normal. 6. Firmware: port → function → protocol/speed. Check the data GPS: satellites; compass: heading changes when you rotate; ESC telemetry: RPM on the motors tab . 7. If there's no data — analyzer on the line: are there bytes, what speed, inversion. practice Step 1. GPS with compass UART + I2C Connect the GPS to UARTx TX↔RX , the compass to SDA/SCL, 5 V power. Betaflight: Ports → GPS on UARTx, Configuration → GPS UBLOX, 57600/115200; enable the magnetometer. ArduPilot: SERIALx_PROTOCOL = 5 , GPS_TYPE = 2 GPS1_TYPE in 4.6+, u-blox , compass — autodetect. Check: NSats ≥ 6 outdoors, the heading rotates. Step 2. ESC telemetry The common telemetry wire from all ESCs → RX of a free UART. Betaflight: Ports → ESC on UARTx, esc_sensor enabled; check — RPM/temperature on the Motors tab without props. ArduPilot: SERIALx_PROTOCOL = 16 . Step 3. A rangefinder or another UART/I2C device Follow the procedure from the theory; check in the firmware ArduPilot RNGFND1_TYPE , Betaflight/INAV — the sensors tab . Step 4. Analyzer Capture one frame: UBX from the GPS header B5 62 , an ESC telemetry byte, or a compass I2C transaction with the address and ACK. What you should get and what to record - Before power-up: with the multimeter — 5 V at the device connector, common ground, TX and RX not swapped the TX of one goes to the RX of the other . 3.3 V and 5 V levels not mixed: a 5 V TX into a 3.3 V RX without level shifting is a path to a fried port. - GPS: in the firmware the satellite count grows and a fix appears. The I²C compass is detected automatically. If not, a bus scanner will show the address: for example, 0x0D QMC5883L , 0x0E IST8310 , 0x1E HMC5883L . - ESC telemetry: in the Motors tab Betaflight

Check the bus with the power off Step 2. Setup and nodes Step 3. DroneCAN GUI Tool Step 4. Conflict and recovery Step 5 (optional). Node firmware update
text: summary On a 5" quad everything lives on UART and I²C. On an X8, a VTOL or any vehicle with wires longer than half a meter, that ends in interference, a shortage of ports and “GPS drops out on throttle”. DroneCAN moves the GPS, compass, current sensor, rangefinders, airspeed and even ESCs onto a single four-wire differential bus. This module is the system level on top of “Connecting peripherals” and “Protocols”: bus physics and checking it with a multimeter, node IDs and their automatic allocation DNA , ArduPilot and PX4 setup, ESCs over CAN and the bus load budget, updating node firmware, and AP_Periph — how to make your own node from an STM32 board. theory Why a bus when you have UART - Noise immunity. CAN is a differential pair: interference couples into both wires equally, and the receiver looks at the difference. A meter of wire next to an X8 power bus is normal for CAN and guaranteed glitches for I²C. - One port, many devices. GPS, compass, current sensor, rangefinder, airspeed, 8 ESCs — on one bus, through a splitter. - Telemetry and diagnostics for free. Every node reports on itself NodeStatus : health, mode, uptime , and the node firmware can be updated from the ground station. - Redundancy. Two CAN ports on the flight controller mean two independent buses; critical nodes are duplicated. The price: more expensive peripherals, slightly more complex setup, and the bus has to be built correctly physically. Bus physics - 1 Mbit/s the DroneCAN standard . The longer the bus, the stricter the requirements; on a vehicle it's a few meters, which is not a limitation. - 120 Ω terminators at both ends of the bus, and only at both ends. Check with the power off: a multimeter between CAN_H and CAN_L should show ~60 Ω two 120 Ω in parallel . 120 Ω means one terminator, infinity means none, 40 Ω means three. - Dronecode/Pixhawk connector : JST-GH 4 pin — 1: +5 V, 2: CAN_H, 3: CAN_L, 4: GND. The H/L pair is twisted. - Topology is a line , not a star: short stubs off the trunk. Splitters CAN hub/splitter make the “line” internally. - Power over the bus: the 5 V from the flight controller is current-limited — a GPS with compass and a couple of sensors are fine, ESCs and servos are powered separately. DroneCAN on top of CAN DroneCAN formerly UAVCAN v0 defines what goes in the frames: the 29-bit frame identifier carries the priority, the message type and the sender's node ID; long messages are split across several frames. The node ID is 1…127; the flight controller is usually 10 in ArduPilot CAN_D1_UC_NODE and 1 in PX4 UAVCAN_NODE_ID . DNA dynamic node allocation : a new node without an ID asks the server for one, and the flight controller hands out a free one and remembers it by the node's unique ID. That's why peripherals “just plug in and work”. It breaks when nodes are moved between vehicles or settings are copied: two nodes with the same stored ID means a conflict. The fix is clearing the DNA table on the flight controller or a fixed ID on the node. Cyphal UAVCAN v1 is the next, incompatible version of the protocol; ArduPilot and most peripherals use DroneCAN, PX4 supports both. When buying peripherals, check that they speak DroneCAN. ArduPilot setup What Parameters Value --- --- --- Enable port CAN1 CAN_P1_DRIVER 1 first driver Driver 1 protocol CAN_D1_PROTOCOL 1 = DroneCAN Bitrate CAN_P1_BITRATE 1000000 GPS over CAN GPS1_TYPE before 4.6 — GPS_TYPE 9 = DroneCAN Current sensor BATT_MONITOR 8 = DroneCAN Rangefinder RNGFND1_TYPE 24 = DroneCAN ESCs over CAN CAN_D1_UC_ESC_BM bitmask of the outputs sent to the bus as ESC commands The node's compass is picked up automatically it shows up in the compass list . After changing CAN_ , reboot. In Mission Planner: Setup → Optional Hardware → DroneCAN/UAVCAN shows the nodes, their parameters and firmware update; that's also where SLCAN mode is, which turns the flight controller into a USB-CAN adapter for DroneCAN GUI Tool. PX4 setup UAVCAN_ENABLE : 2 — sensors, 3 — sensors and ESCs; after that, nodes are discovered automatically, and which data to accept is chosen with the UAVCAN_SUB_ parameters. ESCs over CAN: UAVCAN_ENABLE = 3 , then output mapping on the Actuators tab in QGC. The details differ between versions — check the DroneCAN section of the PX4 docs for your version. ESCs over CAN and bus load The ESC command esc.RawCommand carries 14 bits per motor: for 8 motors that's 14 bytes of payload, i.e. a multi-frame message of ~3 frames. At 400 Hz that's ~1200 frames/s. A CAN frame with 8 data bytes and an extended identifier is ~130–150 bits with bit stuffing; at 1 Mbit/s the bus carries ~7000 frames/s. ESC commands take ~15–20 %, plus ESC telemetry coming back, GPS, compass, current sensor. Rule: keep the bus load below ~50 %, and put ESCs and navigation sensors on different buses if there are many nodes. AP_Periph: your own node AP_Periph is ArduPilot firmware that turns an STM32 board your own or an off-the-shelf one: GPS modules, “CAN adapters” into a DroneCAN node. The same hwdef as flight controllers, and ArduPilot drivers run on the node: GPS, compass, baro, rangefinders, airspeed, LEDs, all the way up to a CAN → PWM/DShot ESC bridge the node takes ESC commands from the bus and outputs them to ordinary ESCs . This is the way to go when you need a CAN sensor that isn't sold. {{diagram:dronecan-bus DroneCAN on a vehicle: a linear bus with 120 Ω terminators at the ends; the flight controller allocates node IDs DNA , GPS, current sensor and ESCs on one pair of wires.}} practice Step 1. Check the bus with the power off Build the bus: flight controller → splitter → GPS/compass → current sensor or any two nodes . Multimeter between CAN_H and CAN_L with the power off: record the resistance. Expect 55–65 Ω. Deliberately remove one terminator — 120 Ω; that's the most common cause of “the node is there, then it isn't”. Step 2. Practice Step 2. Power soldering on the build Step 3. Signal harness Step 3b. Joint resistance by the voltage-drop method Step 4. Routing and securing
text: summary Most “mysterious” failures are a cold solder joint, a chafed wire or a connector that was hanging by a thread. This module is about the craft: how to solder power pads and thin signal wires without cold joints, which solder and flux to use, how to tin, how to strip insulation, route harnesses, secure them and protect them from vibration, and how to check connections mechanically and electrically before flying. theory The physics of soldering Solder wets metal only at a high enough temperature and on a clean surface. Flux dissolves the oxides. A cold joint is solder that set without wetting one of the sides: dull, grainy, balled up. It conducts today and breaks from vibration tomorrow. - Temperature : 330–370 °C for leaded solder Sn63/Pb37, melts at 183 °C , 370–400 °C for lead-free. Big power pads need a big tip and power 60–80 W , otherwise the pad won't heat through and you get a cold joint; small FC pads need a fine tip and brief contact ≤ 3 s , otherwise the pad lifts. - Solder : 0.6–0.8 mm flux-core for signal wires, 1.0 mm for power. Leaded is easier for beginners lower temperature, better flow . - Flux : no-clean or rosin; active acid flux — never on electronics. Rosin residue — wash it off with isopropyl alcohol: it's hygroscopic and can conduct. - Tinning : before joining, tin both the wire and the pad. The joint — press the tinned wire against the tinned pad, heat until they merge, hold still until it sets 1–2 s . Wires - Silicone insulation, stranded — for everything on board: flexible, tolerates soldering-iron heat. - Strip insulation with a gauge-matched stripper, not a knife: nicked strands break. - Tinned length = pad depth; an extra tinned section becomes stiff and breaks at the boundary — the wire should bend at the insulation, not at the joint. - Heat shrink on every exposed section, especially the power ones. Wire gauge: calculate, don't guess A copper wire is a resistor. Resistance per meter 20 °C by gauge: AWG mΩ/m Where on board --- --- --- 10 3.3 battery → PDB on heavy aircraft 60–100 A 12 5.2 6S battery on 10" and X8 14 8.3 battery on 5", phases of powerful motors 16–18 13–21 4-in-1 ESC on 5", phases 20–22 33–53 5 V BEC, VTX, camera 26–28 134–213 UART, I²C signals, sensors Worked example: a 10" on 6S, 60 A peak current, positive and negative 15 cm each 0.3 m of loop . 14 AWG: R = 8.3·0.3 = 2.5 mΩ, a 0.15 V drop, 9 W of heating in the wire at peak. 18 AWG: 0.38 V and 23 W — the wire heats up, the insulation softens, and the drop adds to the battery sag. 12 AWG: 0.09 V and 5.6 W. Conclusion: power gauge is chosen by peak current and length, not “like everyone else”; short power wires are a free voltage bonus. {{widget:wire-drop}} Contact: where you lose more than in the wire A bad joint or an old connector is 1–5 mΩ instead of fractions of a mΩ. At 50 A every extra milliohm is 2.5 W of heat in a spot the size of a pea; the connector plastic melts before anything is noticeable in flight. An XT60 is rated for roughly 30 A continuous more at peak ; for 40–60 A continuous — XT90 or AS150. A connector that's warm after a flight while the wires are cold is a candidate for replacement. Crimping vs soldering Crimping with the right tool gives a gas-tight joint that isn't afraid of vibration; soldering a crimp makes the strands stiff at the edge and the wire breaks next to it. Signs of a bad crimp: strands sticking out of the barrel, the insulation not gripped by the second pair of tabs, the wire rotates. Test: pull with 2–3 kg of force for 26–28 AWG — it shouldn't come out. Connectors Soldering XT30/XT60: connector mated to its pair so the plastic doesn't warp , heat the pads until the solder flows, insert the wire, add more solder. JST-SH/GH pins — crimp, don't solder; crimp with the right tool or buy ready-made harnesses. Connectors under vibration — secure them a drop of hot glue on the housing, not on the pins . Harnesses and vibration - A wire breaks where one point is rigid and the next one isn't: at the joint, at the zip tie. Secure it 3–5 cm from the joint, not right next to it. - A harness has a loose bend, it's not pulled tight especially to an FC on soft mounts . - Chafe protection: sleeving/heat shrink where it touches carbon; sharp frame edges — dress them. - Signal wires — twisted with ground, routed separately from power; power + and − — twisted see interference . - Nothing in the prop zone or in the folding path of a folding frame's arms. Checking 1. Visually : a shiny cone of solder, the wire outline is visible, no balls or bridges. 2. Mechanically : a light pull test on each wire; wiggle it at the joint. 3. Electrically : continuity test of neighboring pads for shorts, the resistance of a power joint — fractions of a mΩ a multimeter can't see it, but heating under load will show it . 4. Under load : props off, throttle for a minute, a thermal camera or a finger carefully on each joint: a hot one is a bad one. 5. Vibration test : motors at low throttle without props for 30 s — nothing rattles or comes loose. {{diagram:wiring-chain A reliable connection: preparation, soldering, strain relief, harness mounting and a check under current.}} practice Step 1. Practice On a scrap board/old ESC: 10 joints with 20 AWG, 10 joints with 28 AWG. Cut one power joint crosswise — the solder should fill the whole cross-section with no voids. Step 2. Power soldering on the build XT60 → PDB/ESC with 14 AWG. Check: pull test, continuity, heating under load without props . Step 3. Signal harness Receiver → FC 5 V, GND, TX, RX : twist, length with slack for bending, secured 3–5 cm from the joint, heat shrink. Step 3b. Joint resistance by the voltage-drop method A multimeter can't measure fractions of a milliohm, but a current plus a millivoltmeter can. A bench power supply in 5 A current-limit mode, pass the current through the power connection XT60 + solder joint , the multimeter probes in mV mode — directly on both sides of the connection.
